articles.title: Pope's South American trip to go ahead as planned after lung cancer surgery
articles.summary: The Pope underwent surgery in to remove a tumour on the lower part of his right lung and is gradually resuming his duties.
body: The Vatican has confirmed that Pope Leo will go on his South American tour as planned, following his surgery for lung cancer.
He was diagnosed with lung cancer and underwent successful surgery in Rome on 13 October to remove a tumour on the lower part of his right lung.
The 71-year-old is scheduled to travel to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on 6-17 November, the Vatican said, adding that the he was looking forward to it "with great joy and enthusiasm".
The Pope will follow the same programme as planned, visiting 10 cities on the tour.
"I am looking forward to returning to the continent where I've experienced so many moments of my life," Pope Leo said.
The Pope's trip will begin in Uruguay on 8 November, where he will visit the capital Montevideo, as well as other key cities.
He will then travel to Argentina from November 11-17, visiting a number of places including the capital Buenos Aires.
After that he will spend six days in Peru, where roughly 76% of the population are Catholic, and will include stops in Lima, Chiclayo, Cuzco and Pucallpa.

Peru's Cardinal Castillo, the Archbishop of Lima, has said the trip would involve young people, women who help run community kitchens and members of the country's indigenous communities, according to Vatican News.
The archbishop highlighted the Pope's close ties with the people of Chiclayo, where he lived for several years. The Pope has Peruvian citizenship.
The Catholic Church sent him to Peru as a missionary in 1985, when he was 30 years old.
He joined the Augustinian mission in Chulucanas, in the Peruvian department of Piura, and the following year, joined the mission in the city of Trujillo.
For almost three decades, he worked between the US and Peru.
The Pope leaving Gemelli Hospital following his lung surgery on 17 October
Leo announced the news of his lung operation himself to the world on 11 October during his weekly Sunday prayers, telling the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a nodule on his lung.
He reassured pilgrims that the growth was "well-contained" and caught "at an early stage" but that his doctors had advised him to have it removed.
The surgery lasted for 90 minutes, and he was discharged from Rome's Gemelli hospital on 17 October.
The Pope's surgeon, Stefano Margaritora, said he was in an "absolutely satisfactory clinical condition", and said there were "no clinical reasons" why the trip should not go ahead.
Tests showed the cancer was "localised".

Since his operation, the pope has been resting and gradually resuming his work. He has been "adjusting his daily schedule in consultation with his doctors to prioritise his recovery while continuing to fulfill the responsibilities of his ministry," the Vatican said.
Leo was "deeply grateful for the prayers and affection he has received from throughout the world," the Vatican said.
The Vatican said Friday that Leo would cancel a planned trip to Assisi on October 27th, on the recommendation of his doctors.

articles.title: Catholic bishops apologise for 'exploited' Trump meeting
articles.summary: Two bishops in images that show them praying with Trump have said they believed the meeting was private.
body: A screengrab of a clip from the 22 October meeting at the White House.

Two Catholic bishops in the US have said they regret meeting President Donald Trump at the White House, after images of them praying with him were released and prompted many to ask if they were making a political statement.
Photos and video of the 22 October meeting show a group of bishops standing around Trump at the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office.
Milwaukee Archbishop Jeffrey Grob, one of those pictured, said he had believed the meeting was private and not "a political photo opportunity".
Trump and Pope Leo XIV have a contentious relationship, and some US bishops have criticised the administration's immigration policies. But Trump has typically enjoyed the support of Catholic voters.

In a statement posted online, Bishop William Joensen of Des Moines, Iowa, said the meeting was arranged by officials with the White House Faith Office to discuss issues including immigration, visas for international clergy and the "exploitation of vulnerable poor persons".
"In no way did any of us intend by our involvement to endorse any political party or any individual candidate," Joensen said.
"I wish I had been more shrewd and less simple, like those who exploited our meeting for partisan political purposes," he added.
A video of the meeting was released by Margo Martin, a special assistant to the president and communications adviser who frequently shares behind-the-scenes images of Trump on social media.
Archbishop Grob said that after 90 minutes of meetings with officials, the religious leaders were ushered into the Oval Office to pray with Trump.
Grob said images of the meeting later caused concern among some of his congregants.
"I soon began receiving messages of serious concern over the possibility that I had inadvertently participated in a political event less than two weeks before a national election," he wrote.
"I also heard from some who felt wounded because of the ways they or their family have been harmed by the president's policies," he added.
Grob said none of the participants in the meeting gave permission for the public distribution or posting of video or photos of the event.
When contacted for comment by the BBC, the White House did not directly address questions regarding the meeting or subsequent comments by the two bishops.
"There has never been a greater president for Catholic Americans than President Trump, and his strong record proves it," White House Spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said in a statement.

According to Pew Research Center, which analyses religion in the US, opinions of Trump's performance have slipped among all major religious groups. In a survey this month, 30% of all US Catholics said they approved of his job performance, compared to 47% when he returned to the White House in 2025.

That could have an effect on the 3 November midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress. More Catholics in the survey, 42%, said they preferred the Democrats running in their local House of Representatives races, where slightly less, 39% favoured Republicans.
During his second term, Trump has had a tense relationship with the head of the Catholic church, Pope Leo, as he has moved aggressively to remove people believed to be in the US illegally.

Nine days before the Oval Office meeting with the bishops took place, Bishop Brendon Cahill and Walter Kim, the president of the National Association of Evangelicals, issued a statement urging "Christian compassion and wisdom in the immigration debate".
They said the immigration clampdown has led to the "sowing of fear, the fracturing of families, the deprivation of due process, and the vilification of our neighbors."
The US Conference of Catholic Bishops also recently condemned the Trump administration's plans to livestream a military execution, which were later scrapped.
Both Vice-President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are Catholics who have visited the Vatican during Trump's second term.
A Midwestern member of the bishops' conference, Robert Barron of Minnesota, agreed to serve on the president's Religious Liberty Commission last year, as did former New York Archbishop Timothy Dolan.

articles.title: Opposition leader María Machado returns from exile to a Venezuela reshaped by Trump
articles.summary: Machado returns with Trump's blessing, even if Washington is happy with Venezuela's existing leader - at least for the time being.
body: Watch: Crowds welcome Venezuela's María Corina Machado after months in exile

Driving down roads lined with jubilant supporters from the western state of Lara to the capital Caracas, Maria Corina Machado's return to Venezuela could hardly have been more different to her exit 10 months earlier.

Colourful, loud, open and defiant, it stood in stark contrast to the way the Venezuelan opposition leader slipped out of the country in the dead of night in December last year to receive the Nobel Peace Prize in Oslo.

She had been unable to make it back to her homeland until now, thwarted on several occasions by the Venezuelan government - and by the Trump administration, which insisted the "time wasn't right" for her return.

"Maria Corina is the indisputable leader of Venezuela," says 20-year-old Gregory Noriega, wearing a sweatshirt emblazoned with the logo of the opposition movement Vente Venezuela. "Her return represents hope."

"This is a step forward in the electoral process which we've been waiting for since last year," echoes 18-year-old Hilary, who turned out on to the streets of the capital hoping to catch a glimpse of the opposition leader on her victory lap.
"She's returned after the double earthquakes when Venezuela needs her," adds her friend, Manuel. "The whole country is behind her to show that now Venezuela isn't scared."
Much has changed since Machado left Venezuelan soil to receive the Nobel Peace Prize.
Then-President Nicolás Maduro is no longer at the top of the Venezuelan government.
Maduro was forcibly removed from power by US troops on 3 January, and whisked to New York where he faces drugs, weapons and torture charges – to which he's pleaded not guilty.
He was replaced by his former vice-president, Delcy Rodríguez, who has turned the page with Washington in ways few could have imagined.
The bilateral relationship is today unrecognisable from the years of mutual animosity during the reigns of President Hugo Chávez and then his handpicked successor, Maduro.
The new circumstances throw up some interesting conundrums for both sides.

When Machado left Venezuela, she had long been considered Washington's favoured alternative to Maduro. She returns to find the Trump administration perfectly happy with the one they've got – at least for the time being.
The Trump administration recently signed a major oil deal with Venezuela which gave the US a 100-year concession over a staggering 65bn barrels of Venezuelan crude oil.
The deal was reached in conjunction with a Venezuelan private company called North American Blue Energy Partners (NABEP) run by a businessman with a chequered past, Alejandro Betancourt.

Machado has openly criticised the deal which the Rodríguez government reached with the US, albeit careful to direct her criticism at Caracas and at Betancourt rather than President Trump, to whom she gave her peace prize and whose trust and support she craves to move forward.

President Trump has repeatedly said how satisfied he is with Delcy Rodríguez, calling her "wonderful" and "a terrific person". This was the vice-president of an administration he previously described as made up of "narco-communists".
But the outpouring of jubilation for Machado's caravan into the capital shows she can still count on significant support on the streets, says Venezuelan political analyst Beningno Alarcon.

"The return of Maria Corina Machado, in my personal view, is the most significant [political] event since 3rd January," says Alarcon. "It means the most important political leader in Venezuela is back in the country."

"The reception for her return shows that her ability to mobilise her support remains intact, which means the opposition in Venezuela now has something very solid: a leadership which is present on the ground as opposed to solely in exile," he says.

Alarcon provides some evidence that the opposition – and the public at large – feel more emboldened since 3 January, a situation he believes will become only more pronounced with Machado's reappearance.
Political analyst Beningno Alarcon

For instance, a joint study by the political think tanks Polis and Nexo suggests that Venezuela saw three times as many street protests in the first nine months of this year as in all of 2025, with demonstrations spanning a range of issues, from politics and working conditions to water supply.
Furthermore, there's evidence that the repression of such protests has reduced by more than half.
In such an environment, the return of a figurehead like Machado can galvanise an electorate that has spent years fearful of the consequences of speaking out.
Her return also needs to be seen within the context of the wider talks brokered by Washington between the Venezuelan government and the opposition towards a negotiated political solution.
Certainly, the US Secretary of State, Marco Rubio, was quick to say her "safe return" to Venezuela was "the direct result of the US-supported reconciliation talks".

The Nobel Peace Prize winner still faces charges in Venezuela ranging from treason to conspiracy of insurrection. For years, she and her supporters have dismissed the charges as politically motivated and baseless.
Young supporters of Maria Machado

Having made at least eight attempts to return to Venezuela by air and by sea before the Trump administration gave her the green light, Machado now knows she has Trump's blessing to be back on home soil – a position Delcy Rodríguez is both unwilling and unlikely to challenge.
She called Machado's return a "show" and the entire cross-country event, which was livestreamed by her supporters over the weekend, was studiously ignored by state television outlets.
But Rodríguez, too, needs a harmonious relationship with Washington if she is to avoid a fate similar to that of her predecessor and indicated she might be prepared to hold talks with Machado.
For as much as Trump has complimented Rodríguez, he has also made it clear that Washington expects nothing less than her full submission and malleability on key issues like energy.
Some reports have even suggested all major decision-making in the oil-rich nation is being largely dictated by Secretary Rubio via regular WhatsApp calls to the interim president.
The young supporters gathered in droves in Caracas to cheer Maria Corina Machado home say their fears of criticising their government or demanding change are vanishing.
Her return marked an irreversible political transition in Venezuela, they insist, one which they could barely fathom when she left for Oslo just a year ago.

articles.title: Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global
articles.summary: The next fortnight sees two elections on different continents. The outcomes will shape geopolitics and the global economy, writes James Landale
body: Israel and the US are both going to the polls - the consequences will be global
In the next week, two sets of elections will be held on two continents, the outcomes of which could have profound consequences for the world.
By a fluke of electoral timetabling, millions of voters around 6,000 miles apart will unite in exercising their democratic rights within days of each other.
Voters in Israel go to the polls on Tuesday to elect a new parliament; a week later, voters in the United States will elect a new Congress.
A former speaker of that Congress, Tip O'Neill, may have once said that "all politics is local". But the consequences of these elections will undoubtedly be global.
For these elections are not just proximate, they are intertwined.
The future governance of Israel will have a lasting impact on the Middle East and wars raging across the region.
And any change in the electoral map of America could shape not just those wars but also the future of the global economy.
Between the two there is a physical connection: the lobby group Republicans Overseas Israel estimates about half a million Israelis with American passports can vote in both polls.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has highlighted his alliance with US President Donald Trump - including in this Likud party election billboard in Tel Aviv

Marc Zell, the group's chairman, said these electors could influence tight races in the US, such as the Michigan senatorial contest, in which he estimated 10,000 absentee ballots would be cast from Israel. "They can really make a difference," he told the BBC.

But the policy connection is perhaps deeper - and most acute regarding the US-Israeli war on Iran. The massive aerial attack, which began in February, destroyed many military targets and killed much of Iran's leadership. But it failed to overthrow the regime which hit back hard across the Gulf and seized control of the Strait of Hormuz and the energy that flowed through it.
The sheer fact of the elections has already shaped decision-making.
Israel's Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has used the campaign to talk up the possibility of launching a fresh attack on Iran.
He has made new claims – without providing evidence – about Iran's nuclear threat, insisting again the Islamic regime must be overthrown.
His aim: to shore up his reputation as a security leader, which took such a battering after the deadly 7 October Hamas-led attacks on Israel.
US President Donald Trump has added to the speculation of renewed attacks on Iran by endorsing Netanyahu's re-election campaign, saying both men should "soon finish the job" in Iran.

Yet for all the sabre-rattling, there have also been contradictory reports that Trump intervened to restrain Netanyahu from attacking Iran before polling day, fearing a fresh spike in energy prices would remind US voters of his unpopular war.
President Trump has been campaigning on behalf of Republican congressional candidates, including in Michigan on Sunday, where there's a tight Senate race

So might an attack on Iran, then, be delayed until after the elections? Israel's media is full of speculation Netanyahu could try to engineer his survival by attacking Iran as caretaker prime minister after the election.

He would argue, so the theory goes, for a government of national unity – involving him – rather than a coalition between opposition parties. Netanyahu has long been seen as a great survivor of Israeli politics. If he were to lose power, he would face an official inquiry into his actions before the October 7 attacks and renewed legal proceedings involving allegations of corruption.

So real is this speculation that Netanyahu's rival, the former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, has already ruled out joining any unity government. Like all mainstream Israeli politicians, Eisenkot sees Iran as an existential threat to Israel and supports military action against the Islamic regime. But he has explicitly warned against escalating the war for political purposes.

Certainly, Trump may be more willing to attack Iran after the midterms if he is unconstrained electorally and hoping to extract himself from the war with one more push. Some analysts believe Iran is so economically weak from the war and economic sanctions that a fresh round of military strikes might encourage Iranians to overthrow the regime. Others see this as yet more wishful thinking. It is a strategy that has repeatedly failed, but still has currency in Washington.
"After the midterms, he will be in legacy mode," one well-placed Western diplomat told me. "He will want to show agency on anything that is not the quagmire at home."

In Israel there is a broad consensus across most parties about the threat from and the need to constrain Iran. But if voters elect a new government, they might have a prime minister with less political and personal investment in fresh attacks.

In those circumstances, Trump has suggested his thinking may change, too. "If Israel has the wrong Leader, which would be anyone other than Bibi [a nickname for Netanyahu], America will have to do this work ourselves, and I am not inclined to do so," he wrote on social media.
Netanyahu has used this year's election campaign to talk up the possibility of a fresh attack on Iran

Little wonder policymakers in Tehran have been following US opinion polls as closely as any analyst inside the Washington beltway. The risk, of course, is that any post-electoral strikes would plunge the Middle East into fresh chaos if Iran were to retaliate hard.
Publicly and privately, Iranian officials have threatened to hit airports, pipelines, undersea cables, energy facilities, desalination plants as well as US bases and warships.
Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, wrote in the Financial Times that new attacks would put "civilian lives and the wellbeing of all regional states and the global economy at great risk".

The two elections again intertwine around the global economy. Affordability and cost of living have dominated campaigning for the midterms, issues made worse by Trump's war that raised prices as Iran choked the flow of energy through the Strait of Hormuz.

The economy is also an election issue in Israel, where voters face high costs and low wages. But here, too, the war plays its part with soaring defence spending putting even more pressure on the public finances.

Trump has sought to appease voters ahead of the midterms. He has lifted sanctions on Russia, hoping in vain that by importing diesel from Moscow, prices might fall significantly. He has been taking a tough line with Ukraine, calling on its leadership to make concessions in the hope – also so far in vain – of claiming a foreign policy victory.

But Republican ire at his controversial strategy is growing. Senator Thom Tillis of North Carolina, a frequent critic of Trump, told CBS News: "If the President wants to actually bring down energy prices, he can do it by solving the Iran problem, not by doing a solid [favour] for Vladimir Putin."
Early voting has already started in many US states for next month's midterms

One consequence of the Iran war – along with Israel's military operations in Gaza and the occupied West Bank – is that traditional bipartisan support in the US has fractured. Abdul El-Sayed, the left-wing Democratic candidate for the Senate in Michigan, campaigns on cutting military aid to Israel. "An ally that takes your money, to push you into wars you shouldn't be fighting, is not an ally," he told ABC News.

The US and Israel initially attacked Iran to destroy its ballistic missiles, degrade its nuclear capability, weaken its support for proxy militias and even oust the entire regime. Since then its war aims have changed to reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

Brad Lander, a Democratic congressional candidate in New York who also sits on the left of his party, chose even to travel to the West Bank only days before polling. He helped Palestinians harvest olives and was briefly detained by Israeli forces, all grist to his social media electoral mill. In the history of US politics, this is not normal. Even Netanyahu is warning that Israel may in future have to survive without a US security blanket.
The leader of Israel's Yashar party, Gadi Eisenkot, has ruled out joining a unity government after the elections

Of course, if Israel's prime minister were to lose, his departure would end a scratchy bromance that has seen Trump blow hot and cold. Last week the president called his Israeli counterpart a "great warrior prime minister". During the summer, he said Netanyahu was "effing crazy". A new Israeli leader would have to forge a new relationship with an outgoing US president, a very different dynamic.

If the Democrats were to win greater control in Congress, that might place some check on blanket US support for Israel. Congress has traditional powers that it can use to restrain military spending. It could also cut military aid to Israel. But as president, Trump would retain significant executive power – and a veto – to continue prosecuting the conflict as he saw fit.

The decision by Israel and the US to go to war with Iran earlier this year transformed the global economy and international geopolitics. The choices voters in both nations make in coming days may shape where the world goes next.

articles.title: How 'Lula's Army' WhatsApp channel helped turn Brazil election around
articles.summary: Millions joined a 'Lula's Army' channel that helped to transform online enthusiasm into real-world mobilisation.
body: Lula's supporters mobilised en masse despite polls pointing to a defeat for the incumbent

A WhatsApp channel created to support Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva's re-election campaign is being credited by allies with helping deliver one of the most unlikely comebacks in recent Brazilian politics.
Brazil's left-wing president had been trailing right-wing challenger Flávio Bolsonaro, but managed to turn the race around in just three weeks.
At a moment when many doubted Lula could reverse the result, a WhatsApp channel called Lula's Army emerged, and rapidly grew to 10.8 million followers.
Led by Congressman André Janones, the operation encouraged supporters to share videos, promote hashtags and recruit new voters.
Its dramatic growth between the two rounds was particularly notable because it appeared to reverse a long-standing imbalance in Brazilian politics.
For years, conservatives aligned with former President Jair Bolsonaro had been widely seen as dominating online political mobilisation, especially on platforms such as WhatsApp and Telegram.
Lula called André Janones "our General" after his major contribution paid off

The emergence of Lula's Army convinced many supporters that Brazil's left had finally found a way to compete in a digital arena. The shift was particularly significant because social media has played a central role in Brazilian politics since Jair Bolsonaro's 2018 election victory, when WhatsApp networks became a defining feature of political campaigning.

Lula's Army messages often included ready-made templates for followers to share with friends and family. Each one assigned supporters a specific task aimed at boosting Lula's visibility on social media.
Janones frequently instructed his "troops" to "blow up" the latest campaign video or help a new hashtag "take off".
"Guys, urgent!", "Don't go to sleep yet", "No food before the mission!", and "I have one more task before you're dismissed", were some of the instructions.
On the eve of the election, the congressman also hosted a 24-hour live event - dubbed the "turnaround livestream" - even as polls continued to suggest a victory for Bolsonaro.

The tactic worked, despite worries by some members of the Workers' Party that Janones's often-confrontational style on social media could undermine the more moderate image they hoped to project for Lula.
In his victory speech, Lula referred to Janones as "our General" and thanked him for "raising the morale of our troops every day".
Measuring the electoral impact of online mobilisation, however, is notoriously difficult.

While Lula's allies credit Lula's Army with helping fuel the comeback, political scientists caution that it is impossible to determine how many votes, if any, were directly influenced by the WhatsApp operation.
Political scientist Denilde Holzhacker argues that a shift in Lula's campaign strategy was key to his comeback.
Rather than relying solely on online engagement, she says the Workers' Party candidate succeeded in connecting digital campaigning with grassroots mobilisation on the ground.

According to Holzhacker, the campaign intensified local efforts and adapted its messaging - linking a Bolsonaro victory with concerns about potential changes to social programmes and the loss of rights.

"It was to Lula's credit that he recognised his own weakness and completely changed his style," she says. "And Janones managed to do something that had seemed unthinkable for Brazil's left - dominate social media."
By contrast, Holzhacker argues that Flávio Bolsonaro entered the run-off overly confident of victory and failed to communicate his message to his supporters as effectively.
Sociologist and political scientist Mayra Goulart, a professor at the Federal University of Rio de Janeiro, also cautions against attributing Lula's comeback solely to social media.
"It was a combination of social media and street-level mobilisation," she says. "The physical world enabled a form of mobilisation capable of reducing abstention and persuading undecided voters."
In her view, Lula's supporters succeeded in turning online enthusiasm into real-world political engagement.
"Those committed to Lula's victory worked to bring people together and persuade them to vote," Goulart says.
She argues that the effort not only helped increase turnout but could also prove valuable for Lula's next administration.

"I believe this collective effort was an important learning experience and will prove valuable for a government that still faces many battles ahead. It not only helped reduce abstention, but also converted a significant number of undecided voters."
Lula himself suggested that the mobilisation behind his comeback could shape the way he governs in the years ahead.
In his victory speech, he said the election had taught him many lessons and pledged to change the way Brazil is governed.
"We are going to give people a greater say in decision-making, and digital communication will play a much bigger role in my government."

articles.title: Who is Lula? From ex-worker and prisoner to Brazil's president again
articles.summary: The firebrand left-winger, who has at times been at odds with Trump, has won his fourth term as Brazil's president.
body: Even for a veteran politician like Lula, uniting a divided nation will be a challenge
On the face of it, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has done the impossible one more time - within three weeks he overturned defeat in first-round voting to gain re-election as Brazil's president.
It was no mean achievement for a man who before his first successful run at the post in 2002 had tried three times unsuccessfully.
When he became president in 2003, he came to office as the first leftist leader of Brazil in nearly half a century.

Now aged 80 and with plenty of experience at governing as large a democracy as Brazil, he has bucked the trend of electoral victory for right-wing leaders in Latin America whose policies mirror that of US President Donald Trump.
Lula's first presidential victory in 2002 marked the end of an unprecedented journey from poverty.
The son of a poor, illiterate peasant family, Lula worked as a peanut seller and shoe-shine boy as a child, only learning to read when he was 10 years old.
He went on to train as a metalworker and found work in an industrial city near São Paulo, where he lost the little finger of his left hand in an accident in the 1960s.
Lula was not initially interested in politics, but threw himself into trade union activism.

Elected leader of the 100,000-strong Metalworkers' Union in 1975, he transformed trade union activism in Brazil by turning what had mostly been government-friendly organisations into a powerful independent movement.

In 1980, Lula brought together a combination of trade unionists, intellectuals, Trotskyites and Church activists to found the Workers' Party (PT), the first major socialist party in the country's history.
The PT went on to gradually replace its revolutionary commitment to changing the power structure in Brazil with a more pragmatic, social democratic platform.
Lula came to power promising major reforms to the country's political and economic system.
He vowed to eradicate hunger and create a self-confident, caring, outward-looking nation.
In this picture Lula is seen meeting fellow Polish trade unionist - and subsequently president - Lech Walesa in Rome, Italy, in 1981
In his time in office, Lula pumped billions of dollars into social programmes and can reasonably claim to have helped reverse Brazil's historic inequalities.

By increasing the minimum wage well above the rate of inflation and broadening state help to the most impoverished with a family grant programme, the Bolsa Familia, he helped some 44 million people and cemented his support among the poor.
However, many commentators argue that the programme failed to address the structural problems that underpin poverty, such as a lack of education.

He left office eight years later, after serving two terms as president, enjoying exceptionally high popularity ratings for a retiring Latin American leader - 83% - having raised Brazil's profile on the international scene and presided over the longest period of economic growth in three decades.

Unable to run for a third term, Lula left the presidency and, shortly afterwards, was diagnosed with throat cancer. He even shaved his trademark beard during treatment. Doctors declared him cured of the disease in 2012.
Lula wins fourth term in dramatic Brazil election comeback
Lula faces hostile congress and divided country after Brazil election win

Under his chosen successor, progress stalled. The economic boom also gave way to recession, and the country's political scene was rocked by a huge investigation into top-level corruption, known as Operation Car Wash.

Lula was among those to get caught up in the scandal. In July 2017, he was convicted of corruption and sentenced to more than nine years in prison for accepting a beachside flat as a bribe from engineering firm OAS - a sentence increased on appeal to 12 years.

Lula was also jailed for 12 years and 11 months for corruption and money laundering for receiving bribes from two construction and engineering firms by way of funding improvements in a country house he and his family used.
He has always maintained his innocence, insisting accusations against him were politically motivated.
In 2019, he was released after having served just over 18 months, after a Supreme Court ruling that the incarceration had been illegal, having come before all appeals had been exhausted.
Those convictions were annulled in 2021, leaving Lula free to run for a third term in 2022, beating right-winger Jair Bolsonaro.
When he re-entered office in 2023, he vowed it would be his last term, and yet his party endorsed him as their candidate again this year, even though he will turn 81 on Tuesday.
Even backers of the PT will acknowledge that he achieved more in his first two terms - from January 2003 to December 2010 - than in his most recent four years in office.

And while his supporters described him ahead of the 2022 election as the "saviour of the Amazon", praising his commitment to protecting the rainforest, some environmentalists have been critical of some of his recent actions.
His support for exploratory oil drilling in offshore waters near the mouth of the Amazon in particular has drawn criticism.
Lula insists that he remains committed to eventually phasing out fossil fuels and argues that oil revenues are key to financing Brazil's transition to clean energy.

His government has also pointed to the reduction in deforestation in the Amazon - satellite data suggests the area deforested in the first half of 2026 was reduced to its lowest in the past decade - as proof that its policies were working.
Lula's third term coincided with the return to office of Trump.
The two men represent different ends of the political spectrum and have found it impossible not to voice their differences in public.
The Brazilian leader told the BBC in September 2025 that he had no relationship with Trump.

Even though the US has a trade surplus with Brazil, Donald Trump imposed 50% tariffs on Brazilian goods in July that year, citing the trial on coup charges of Brazil's right-wing former president Jair Bolsonaro as a trigger. Bolsonaro is serving a 27-year jail sentence and it was his son, Flávio, who Lula beat in Sunday's election run-off.

Lula accused Trump of foreign interference and said "he's not emperor of the world". But their relationship improved after a White House in May this year, after which the two leaders exchanged public compliments - Trump called Lula "dynamic", while the Brazilian president said he left the meeting "very satisfied".
In July of this year, the US imposed 25% tariffs on most goods, external from Brazil.
The two governments still disagree on key issues such as crime, and Lula acknowledged they are especially far apart on trade.

Referring to what Trump has dubbed the "Donroe doctrine" - his administration's national security strategy which asserts that US dominance in the Western hemisphere should not be interfered with - Lula has insisted that "Brazil does not fit into anyone's backyard".
Trump and Lula had warm words when they met in Washington earlier this year

Lula has criticised the fact that five countries - the permanent members of the UN Security Council - have the power to veto decisions and argued that this tilted the balance in favour of those who won World War Two, excluding nations representing billions of people like Brazil, Germany, India, and Japan, as well as African countries.
Brazil is an active member of the Brics - a grouping that unites Brazil with Russia, India, China and South Africa.
Lula defends his continued alliances with Russia and China and sees the Brics as an emerging counterweight to the West.
He has defended his choice to continue to purchase Russian oil while Russia wages war in Ukraine.

articles.title: Five ways Trump has changed immigration in the US
articles.summary: This is how his signature policy has played out after returning to power promising a closed border and mass deportations.
body: Immigration has always been central to Donald Trump's message.

When he famously stepped onto the golden escalator at Trump Tower to announce his candidacy for his first presidential term in 2015, he accused Mexico for of sending drugs and crime north of the border - and it's been a constant rallying cry ever since.
Some of his first-term ambitions to stem the flow of would-be immigrants were constrained by the courts.
But restraints have been weaker in his second term, with a more accommodating Supreme Court and tens of billions of additional enforcement money from Congress.
Who should be allowed to live in the US remains a big issue on the minds of voters in the upcoming midterm elections, which are largely seen as a referendum on the Trump presidency.
He promised a closed border and mass deportations in his successful 2024 campaign - and few can deny that he's delivered on both.
But even among those who voted for a tougher stance, there is a concern that the crackdown has gone too far.
His signature policy has played out in five key ways.

Crossings exploded during Joe Biden's presidency, with over 4.5 million migrant "encounters" recorded at the southern border in 2023 and 2024 alone, reflecting the massive numbers of people headed north to the US border.
His administration eventually brought the monthly figures down significantly by restricting asylum claims and removing migrants entering the US illegally without processing.
When Trump returned to office, that stream of migrants became a trickle. Border encounters plummeted.
By the end of Trump's first year in office, the chaotic scenes that had generated headlines around the globe during the Biden administration had largely gone.

On a trip to the border city of El Paso, Texas, in November 2025, for example, the BBC found quiet streets where there had previously been makeshift camps housing thousands of migrants granted parole in the US to await immigration proceedings.
To achieve what he often describes as the "most secure" border in US history, the Trump administration has taken an aggressive, multi-pronged approach.

That has included effectively freezing asylum applications at the border, ending "catch and release" of detainees into the US, deploying troops to the border and pressuring Mexico to clamp down on the flow of migrants headed north.
"President Trump promised the American people a secure border, and the data proves he delivered," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement on 16 October.
"The results could not be clearer: strong enforcement works."
A vow to build a "big, beautiful wall" at the nearly 2,000-mile (3,218km) US-Mexico border was a signature promise of Trump's 2016 campaign.
Progress on it has speeded up in his second term, boosted by $46.5bn (£34.7bn) in new funding from Trump's "One Big Beautiful" spending bill.

According to government figures, external, about 644 miles of "primary wall" - closest to the border - existed before Trump returned to the White House, in addition to 75 miles of "secondary" wall set slightly further inside the US.

Since then, 250 more miles of new wall have been completed, including primary, secondary and waterborne barriers, along with the technology that helps detect illegal crossings. An additional 1,443 miles of barriers are currently under construction.
Experts, however, paint a more complex picture of what has been actually built rather than just improved or updated.
Additionally, the impact the wall is itself having on the broader immigration figures is up for debate.

"Since new wall construction has really begun in earnest, there has been no significant change in the number of people crossing the border," said Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, an immigration enforcement expert at the American Immigration Council.
There is no indication the border wall has reduced migrant crossings, he added. The reduction has been more down to Trump's policies and messaging.
Trump, for his part, continues to point to the wall as a successful policy - and continues to claim that Mexico paid for it.

"I'm the King of the Wall," Trump said at a rally in Kentucky on 17 October. "By the way, Mexico did pay for that wall. I charged them tariffs and I charged them costs like they've never paid in history."
Hispanic voters helped bring Trump to power - in Texas, the tide may be turning

Most of the headlines generated by Trump's immigration policies have come from the US interior, where operations by Immigrations and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents to round up people they say are in the US illegally have rocked cities across the country.

During his campaign, Trump promised an immediate start to what he described as the "largest deportation operation in American history", which officials said would begin with people who have committed crimes first.

Arrests - and subsequent detentions in immigration facilities - have shot up significantly since Trump returned to office, including a record of nearly 50,000 in July this year alone, according to data obtained by the Deportation Data Project, external, a repository of US immigration data run out of University of California, Berkeley, and UCLA.

But the same data, external shows that a large chunk of the arrests involve people without criminal convictions. In July 2026, detentions of immigrants with criminal histories reached an all-time low of 27%.

Deportations have also ramped up significantly. By mid-July this year, ICE was removing an average of 1,255 people from the country per day, compared to about 770 in Biden's final months in office - although Biden's own removals had sharply risen in his final year in office.

But the tactics used by ICE in US cities have made many Americans grow uncomfortable, including many of those who supported stricter restrictions broadly. This became increasingly evident following Operation Metro Surge, a two-month large scale enforcement action in Minneapolis in early 2026 that left two US citizens dead.

A New York Times and Siena poll, external released on 21 October found that 50% of voters trust Democrats to handle the issue, compared with 46% for Republicans - despite the issue being a traditional Republican strength.

A separate poll, from Politico and Public First, external in late September, found deep splits between Republicans on the issue, with 31% of non-MAGA Republicans, meaning those not aligned with Trump's movement, believing that campaign has become too aggressive.
Watch: Texas voters share concerns over cost of living ahead of midterms
After returning to the White House last year, Trump almost immediately suspended refugee admissions, saying at the time these could only restart if they were shown to be in US interests.

In February, however, an executive order signed by Trump narrowly re-opened that process for Afrikaners from South Africa, who the White House has repeatedly said are being killed and "persecuted" - a claim that the government in Pretoria has denied.

The cap for refugee admissions for the 2026 fiscal year was initially set at 7,500, which was raised to 17,500 in May this year because of what the administration described as an "unforeseen emergency refugee situation".
Overall refugee admissions have slowed to a relative trickle. State Department data shows that 16,292 refugees were admitted into the US in the 2026 fiscal year - of whom 16,287 were South African.

By comparison, in the final two fiscal years of the Biden administration - 2023 and 2024 - 60,000 and 100,000 entered the country, respectively. In the 2024 fiscal year, the highest numbers came from Democratic Republic of Congo, Afghanistan, Syria and Venezuela.

Hundreds of thousands of people protected from deportation lost that protection when a humanitarian protection called Temporary Protected Status (TPS) was also ended in Trump's second term. It gave vetted individuals the right to live and work in the US if their home countries were deemed to be unsafe to return to.
One of those countries was Haiti. In June, the Supreme Court upheld the Trump administration's decision to end TPS for some 350,000 Haitians in the US.
Haitian migrants changed this US town - Trump's deportation drive is reshaping it again
Other legal pathways to come to live and work in the US have also been tightened up, through various policy changes.
Dozens of countries the Trump administration has deemed a security risk have been subject to a full or partial freeze on visas and travel.
Enhanced vetting and new rules that send people residing in the US back to their home countries to apply for green cards has slowed that process down.

And in September 2025, a $100,000 fee on new H1-B visas for skilled workers, mostly held by Indians, stunned the US tech industry. In May this year, the US Citizenship and Immigration Services said on X, external that registrations for 2027 were down 40%.

"The data is a clear sign that the days of abusing the program with mass, low-wage registrations are over, and that the program is better serving its intended purpose of attracting highly skilled foreign workers and protecting the wages, working conditions and job opportunities of American workers," the statement added.

While a court has blocked the $100,000 fee - for now - the threat of it appears to have deterred employers. But some experts have cautioned the administration's aim of protecting American jobs, raising wages and stopping firms from outsourcing may prove elusive.

One study, from the Wharton School of Business, external, found that the H1-B changes would have "no significant impact" on the wages of US-born workers, with any reduction in competition offset by reduced productivity growth.
Other pathways to the US have been opened, however - if you have a spare million.
The "Trump Gold Card" launched in 2025 sought to entice wealthy foreigners to come live in the US in exchange for a $1m "gift" to the US government, plus a non-refundable $15,000 application fee.
At the time, Trump said that the programme would boost the US economy. Its uptake, however, appears to be minimal so far. By April, only one applicant had been accepted.

articles.title: China's big political meeting could see Xi 'tighten discipline' in party
articles.summary: The highly secretive four-day Plenum starts Monday in Beijing.
body: Plenums are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year
A major political gathering is under way in the Chinese capital, with a closed-door meeting of senior figures that could shape the look of the ruling Communist Party in the years to come.
The Fifth Plenum brings together around 300 members of the Central Committee and state media said it would pave the way for a "tightening of discipline" within the Party's ranks.
The four-day session that started on Monday will give Xi Jinping an opportunity to further consolidate his grip on power following recent purges.
The normally annual plenums are highly secretive, but a summary of decisions and a more detailed document will be made public after.
They are essentially closed door meetings of the Party's central committee that happen at least once a year.
There are usually seven plenums during each five-year Central Committee term and they are watched from afar because they are meant to signal the leadership's priorities.
The timing for this year's gathering is important because it is a year away from the next Party Congress, where a new set of priorities is set up and a new central committee appointed.
Officially, the Central Committee selects the Party's top leadership but the real processes leading to the selection are kept secret within the Party elite.
The next Party Congress will almost certainly reappoint Xi as the country's leader, following the abolition of term limits.

Past plenum sessions have been used to declare Xi as "the core" of the Party, abolish term limits which cleared the way for him to remain in power indefinitely, and elevate his personal philosophy – branded as "Xi Jinping Thought" – to the same level as Chairman Mao.
This year's plenum is an opportunity for Xi to dictate strategy in the run up to the Congress, ensuring that views are aligned and delegates loyal.
Even the location of the meeting, which will wrap up on Thursday, has not been announced. Past plenums have been held inside Beijing's Jingxi Hotel.

According to a readout from the powerful 21-member Politburo this September, the plenum will adopt a decision on "several major issues persistently advancing the comprehensive strict governance of the Party", which is being read as a way to further ensure obedience and effectiveness from distant party officials.
This means it would also be a time of nervousness for delegates as they look around the room with its "empty chairs" following the scale of recent purges within the Party.
Allegations of corruption, even "moral corruption", have seen large swathes of senior figures culled.
"Moral corruption" has been seen by experts as a way of cracking down on perceived disloyalty to Xi because overall disloyalty to the Party can be interpreted as a breach of "morality".
The Asia Society Policy Institute has estimated that of 44 military members appointed to the Central Committee in 2022 only two have not been taken down.
The all-powerful seven-man Central Military Commission, which runs the armed forces in China, has also been whittled down to only two people, Xi Jinping and one other general.
This plenum is an opportunity for him to appoint new officers to this body.

articles.title: Melting glaciers in Dolomites reveal cache of first world war munitions
articles.summary: Italian army removes and defuses 250 explosives encased in ice for more than 100 years after hikers’ sightings
body: A significant cache of unexploded bombs from the first world war emerged this summer from rapidly retreating glaciers in the Dolomites, the Italian army has said.
The devices, which included Italian artillery shells and French mortar bombs, were removed and defused by the army’s Julia Alpine brigade, according to a statement.
The weapons originated from the white war, a battle between the Austro-Hungarian army and Italian troops across treacherous and bitterly cold terrain between 1915 and 1918.

More than a century later, hikers reported several sightings of bombs during the summer, mostly in the area of Canal San Bovo in the Primiero Valley in eastern Trentino. The soldiers then conducted an extensive sweep there and across other high-altitude and glacier locations in the Trentino Alto Adige region of the Dolomites.

They recovered and neutralised 250 explosives, including “18 Italian 75mm artillery shells and 37 Thevetot mortar shells – a French-made device that was also supplied to the Italian royal army during the first world war”, the Julia Alpine brigade.
It is not the first time that relics of the white war have emerged from melting glaciers, whose retreat has accelerated over more than decade.

“It is very much a consequence of global heating,” said Stefano Morosini, a professor at the University of Bergamo and the coordinator of heritage projects at Stelvio national park, where some of the explosives were also found.

“In recent years, at the end of each summer, these dangerous artefacts emerge and each year there is a higher number. They have been conserved by the ice for more than 100 years. Some had already exploded but many hadn’t, so now when they re-emerge, they are very, very dangerous.”
The advice to hikers and mountaineers is to “never touch any type of explosive device you might find, regardless of where it is located” and to promptly report any discovery to police.

Fought mainly in the Dolomites of Trentino Alto-Adige and the Alps of the Lombardy region, the white war was a period of history frozen in time until the 1990s, when global heating started to reveal an assortment of perfectly preserved relics, including weapons, sledges, letters and diaries.
Related: Melting ice reveals first world war relics in Italian Alps

A wooden barracks that had been dug into a cave on the top of Mount Scorluzzo, a 3,095-metre (10,154ft) peak overlooking the Stelvio pass, reappeared in 2015 after the ice which had sealed it off for almost a century completely melted.

The shelter had been hastily locked up when the first world war ended in November 1918, and the soldiers abandoned most of their belongings. Beds made of straw as well as clothes, lanterns, newspapers, postcards, coins, and tinned food were found well preserved inside.
A white war museum to host the relics is scheduled to open in Bormio in June 2027.
The white war is thought to have claimed more than a million lives, although the majority of soldiers were believed to have been killed by avalanches, falling down mountains or hypothermia.
Dozens of corpses, some still in their uniforms, have emerged from the melting ice over the past 15 years.
The relatives of an Italian soldier were able to bury him in 2017 after documents revealing his identity were found with his body on Presena glacier.
Morosini said the intense summer heat was making access to the glaciers in the Dolomites less safe. Eleven people died when a huge mass of the Marmolada glacier broke off in 2022.
“It is becoming more and more impossible to access the glaciers during the summer because of the very long heatwave at high altitude,” he said.
“If you come to the area, you can see how fast the glaciers are retreating and how strong the impact of climate change is.”

articles.title: Tuesday briefing: How a journalistic hunch revealed the scale of Britain’s problematic cocaine use
articles.summary: In today’s newsletter: Once associated with the wealthy, the drug has become omnipresent, with new Guardian analysis revealing rising crime, record deaths and a troubling link to domestic abuse
body: How did Britain become a cocaine nation? Our series investigating how a drug once associated with affluence and exclusivity has become an everyday habit, in pubs, dinner parties, festivals and workplaces, has the answer.
The series reveals that the surge in consumption in recent years has coincided with a 10% increase in related crimes, record deaths and domestic abuse.

This is the kind of original reporting in which journalists put a hunch to the test: supporting their conclusions with a scrupulously analysed dataset and a revelatory source, uncovering some surprising new insights in the process.

But how does that journalistic process work, from premise to publication? I spoke to north of England correspondent Robyn Vinter and data journalist Michael Goodier, the duo behind the investigation, to find out more. But first, the headlines.
UK news | The controversial rule that led to unpaid carers being punished with penalties amounting to thousands of pounds is to be abolished, the Guardian can reveal.

Economy | Shop price inflation has risen to the highest level in two and a half years, according to the British Retail Consortium, which warned that “the dam is starting to break” when it comes to retailers trying to limit price rises.

Serbia | Serbia’s triumphant but untested Student List movement is preparing to start talks on forming a government capable of reversing 14 years of increasingly authoritarian nationalist rule, after a seismic weekend election win.

Israel | Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.
Russell Brand | Russell Brand had an “insane sexual appetite” and his bad behaviour was “normalised and dismissed” by those around him, his former personal assistant has told a court.

Robyn had been watching the gradual uptick in cocaine use from survey data out of the corner of her eye for a few years, but the event that galvanised her interest came in 2021 when thousands of ticketless football fans stormed Wembley stadium during the postponed Euro 2020 final.

A review published in the aftermath of the disorder found that more than half of fans said they had seen cocaine use either inside Wembley stadium or on the way from the station. “I thought ‘God, that’s remarkable that people felt confident to take it so openly’,” Robyn tells me.

Then came the anti-immigration riots of 2024: Robyn noticed that some of the perpetrators of violence were also facing cocaine-related charges. She later observed open cocaine use among marchers at Tommy Robinson’s Unite the Kingdom rally in London. And when she covered Glastonbury for the Guardian last year, “people were taking coke in the crowd in front of everyone,” – par for the course at a music festival, you might think – but Robyn noticed a difference: “a few years ago people were a bit more careful about hiding it.”

Robyn began to wonder whether cocaine use might be at an all time high – and, considering its well recorded effects as a drug that causes paranoid and impulsivity, she asked herself: what might the overall effect on society be from all this?
From theory to numbers: ‘It was one of those journalistic hunches’

Those were the ideas that Robyn brought to Michael, who began to dig into the available data, first sending freedom of information requests to all 45 territorial police forces in the UK. (Please don’t skip over this bit: as someone who has FOIed the 45 herself, and chased up, and chased again, I appreciate what a task that is.)

Michael discovered that police forces across Britain had recorded a 10% rise in recorded crimes in which the class A drug was mentioned since 2019, while the Home Office estimates that cocaine use at sites across England has risen by 26% since 2021.

The data also showed that the record-breaking rise in cocaine use was associated with crimes ranging from assault to dangerous driving, and Robyn had a particular theory she wanted to explore about domestic abuse: “It was one of those journalistic hunches: what’s it like to be in a relationship with somebody who is taking a lot of cocaine?” She contacted domestic violence specialists who explained that, while cocaine use doesn’t make a non-violent person violent, it can make an offender more likely to act on their impulse to do harm.

Again, Michael’s data work suggested Robyn’s suspicions were correct: Home Office figures show nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse tested positive for cocaine use between July 2025 and June this year.
Parsing the data: ‘sewage doesn’t lie’

Assessing data on illegal drug use is tricky, Michael explains, because some people may not want to admit to taking drugs. Crime survey data – which asks individuals about their habits – suggests the number of people reporting cocaine use has fallen slightly since the pandemic. But that’s completely different to analysis of wastewater by Home Office scientists, which shows a significant rise in cocaine levels in sewage, up 26% between 2021 and 2025.

“It’s always important to speak to experts in the field about which data they think is more representative,” Michael tells me. One such expert is Dr Josh Torrance, a specialist in drug markets, who thought the direction of travel shown in the wastewater analysis was broadly accurate. “Sewage doesn’t lie,” says Michael.

The plummeting price of cocaine – apparently the only consumer good exempt from the cost of living crisis – was evidently a factor in its growing use, but assessing this data presented another challenge. Torrance shared price data he had gathered from online drug dealers who ply their trade on Telegram channels and other forums. “Obviously that’s illegal behaviour, so we had to agree with him about which data he was willing to share, and what we were able to publish, to make sure we weren’t exposing any sources in the process.”

A running theme of the reporting is the way that cocaine use has become normalised, moving from being the drug of choice for the affluent to something snorted off the toilet cistern in the local pub. But its apparent omnipresence doesn’t make it any easier to talk about.

Robyn struggled to find anyone willing to be interviewed about their cocaine use, past or present, without using a pseudonym. During her research, she headed to a music festival in the north of England. “I was chatting to people about what drugs they were on, and people just thought I was a cop. People are so cagey about it – understandably – which does make things difficult in terms of reporting.”

All of her interviews for this investigation were done anonymously. “You’re working for the reader and want to give them all the facts you can, but you also want to make it easier for people to speak to you. Sometimes it doesn’t matter precisely what someone’s name is or where in the country they are located.”

Illegality can also be a barrier to seeking help, as she discovered when she interviewed a survivor of cocaine-fuelled domestic violence. It can also prevent businesses affected by cocaine use from working together. She spoke to one pub manager who told her the ubiquity of cocaine has become “significantly worse” over the past five years. “She sees it causing fights and conflict between customers in her pub, but she can’t turn to colleagues for advice on dealing with it because the rules are so strict, she’s worried she’d lose her licence if it got about that there was drug-taking on her premises.”

Michael tells me he’d expected to see a rise in crime in the datasets he was examining, “but the thing that I hadn’t considered before was the age of the cohort taking cocaine.” People in their 30s were the largest age group seeking help with problematic cocaine use. “It is older people now who are taking it for longer, and we’re seeing record deaths. I didn’t expect that, but sadly it makes sense.” Experts told Michael they’d like to see more investment in earlier drug education and addiction services to stem this rise.

It’s a seam that Robyn is keen to mine in future reporting. “When you look at the detailed demographics, there are a lot of young black men that die from overdosing on cocaine.” Robyn suspects these lads are working as drug mules, and die when a package of powder cocaine bursts inside them.
“In this investigation, we’ve focused on the crimes perpetrated by the users. Next I want to look at the crimes and other harms that are happening because of the drugs trade itself,” she says.

The Mirror splashes “It’s time to pay fair” on calls for a windfall tax, the Mail writes “PM’s new foot in mouth Brexit blunder”, and the i Paper leads with “Cabinet anger after Burnham opens door to EU free movement”. Historic win for Lula over far-right Bolsonaro in Brazil

Brazil’s Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva has won a historic fourth term as president, defeating the far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro in a dramatic comeback. Lula is the first candidate to win a runoff election after losing in the first round, taking victory with 51.79% of the vote to his rival’s 48.21%. His win bucks a regional trend, after the son of the former president Jair Bolsonaro had spearheaded a radical populist movement. But with Flávio Bolsonaro refusing to concede defeat, what’s next for Brazil? Michael Safi speaks to Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips.
A bit of good news to remind you that the world’s not all bad

Oxford Street is Europe’s busiest shopping street, but it’s also become one of its least inviting, populated by empty stores and mysterious vape shops. On Sunday evening, almost a kilometre of the street became officially “traffic free”. Over the next few months, it will be planted with new trees and redesigned around public plazas and spaces for music and art events. The idea, the mayor of London Sadiq Khan wrote in the Guardian yesterday, is to “restore this beloved street to its former glory.”
