articles.title: ‘It’s the smell of freedom’: Belgrade cleans up after Student List triumph
articles.summary: Binbag-wielding volunteers clear encampment used by thugs to intimidate opponents of deposed government
body: Student List cleaned up at Serbia’s parliamentary elections. So it was only fitting that the morning after a night of raucous celebrations, the movement’s supporters were gathering, bin bags in hand, at Pioneers Park, opposite the national assembly building in Belgrade.

For the previous 18 months, this small patch of greenery – with its established trees and playground – had been a no-go zone. A pro-government camp known as Ćaciland had taken over the space with convicted criminals living there in white tents, happy to attack journalists, or anyone else who came too close. Police stood by but did nothing to prevent the violence.

On election night, it seemed that thuggery might be on the cards again. Half an hour before the polls closed, large numbers of masked, black-clad men started gathering in and around Pioneers Park. Their intimidating presence gave credence to pre-poll predictions that the governing Serbian Progressive party (SNS) would not hand over power without a struggle.

What happened next took almost everyone by surprise. Shortly after the polls closed – and before any projections of the results had been published – Aleksandar Vučić told supporters at SNS headquarters that they had suffered a comprehensive defeat to the Student List. As cheers rang around the heart of Belgrade, he added that he did “not want unrest” or “anything like that on the streets”.

The riot police stood aside and the barriers blocking access to the area around Pioneers Park were removed. The goon squad made a rapid exit – and Student List supporters joyfully ransacked Ćaciland, setting fire to some of the tents.

But this is not a movement that likes to leave a mess. Over the two years of anti-corruption protests that led to the Student List’s victory, participants have always cleaned up after themselves. So the call went out for volunteers to restore Pioneers Park to something approaching its previous state.

Hundreds of people answered the appeal and joined municipal workers to remove the remains of Ćaciland. Some dismantled the mangled white tents, while others painstakingly cleaned and disinfected the climbing frames, swings and slides in the children’s playground.

Radomir Dalic painstakingly combed over the grass to remove cigarette butts and other rubbish. Apparently relishing his labours, he said he was overjoyed that the park was finally rid of “criminals with violent intentions towards us”.
“Yesterday was a big victory, so today is the smell of freedom,” he added. “We are in garbage, but it’s the smell of freedom.”

Tamara Tomic wore yellow rubber gloves for the occasion – and radiated similar pride in taking part. “Gathering here and cleaning this place just shows that we want to live nicely,” she said. “We want to enjoy the city, enjoy a normal life without violence and without anyone torturing us.”

For now, nobody is asking too many questions about how the Student List will govern. In fact, Serbian voters have taken something of a leap into the unknown – because this is a movement that operates unlike a traditional political party. It has no hierarchy and no leader. Its candidates were chosen by a series of student assemblies, with nominations ranging from academics to athletes, economists to engineers.

The Student List did publish an 11-point plan. Most of these points deal with anti-corruption measures – ironically, the pitch that secured victory in 2012 for Vučić and the SNS. Other commitments include judicial reform, media freedom, affordable housing and improved access to healthcare, with the promise of “a doctor in every village”.

But beyond the domestic priorities – in essence, a clean-up for public institutions – little is clear. The Student List went into the elections without naming a candidate for prime minister, let alone a possible cabinet.

Kurt Bassuener, co-founder of the Democratization Policy Council, said he was concerned about what that might mean when the euphoria of victory died down, and the serious business of forming a government began.

The thinktank chief added: “I’m hoping that there is a dream scenario plan here – they have portfolios and people who have credibility in particular issue areas and they can hit the ground running. Because the danger of a broad coalition like this is that the fissures will show soon after victory.”

Ilija Srdanović, the candidate ranked first on the Student List, has played down the potential for strife. A cardiologist at the university in Novi Sad, the city where a deadly roof collapse sparked the student protests, he has protested alongside the students since the early days. However, he was keen to emphasise that his ranking on the list did not mean he would become prime minister.
“The student movement is fully democratic,” he said, adding that the aim was to buck Serbia’s history of “creating the cult of personality or leadership”.
The 250 candidates on the Student List were “equal subjects in this struggle”, Srdanović insisted, with “numerous candidates who can be chosen for the prime minister position or any other position”.

But his confidence does little to reassure those who have noticed that the broad spread of views held by Student List candidates could lead to trouble. Despite Vučić’s warnings that a Student List government would impose sanctions on Russia and recognise Kosovo’s unilateral declaration of independence, the movement’s foreign and regional policy remains opaque.
“We have not seen seas of EU flags at demonstrations by students or the marches across Serbia,” said Michael Davenport, a former EU and UK ambassador to the country.

“There are massive policy areas where there is no consensus among the Student List or those have been elected. The approach towards accession to the European Union is not clear, nor is the position with regard to regional issues like Bosnia and Herzegovina and, very particularly, Kosovo.”

Many people are happy to leave these concerns for another day. Vučić and the SNS have fallen – and the cacophony of car horns continued throughout Monday as drivers passed the clean-up crew in Pioneers Park.
One visible symbol of the old regime has been swept away. The Student List voters are hoping more will follow.

articles.title: ‘We want a full apology for slavery’: Commonwealth at a crossroads as king heads to the Caribbean
articles.summary: Campaigners say tour could hasten Charles’s removal as head of state unless he does more to confront monarchy’s historic role in slave trade
body: King Charles’s upcoming Caribbean tour could accelerate moves to remove him as head of state in several countries unless he does more to confront the monarchy’s historic links to slavery, campaigners have warned.
The king will embark on a nine-day tour on Tuesday, visiting the Bahamas and Guyana before travelling to Antigua and Barbuda, and will attend the Commonwealth heads of government meeting (Chogm).
Related: King Charles urged ‘as human brother’ to support reparations talks at Caribbean summit

Patrick Vernon, a cultural historian and UK representative of the Global Jamaica Diaspora Council, said the stakes for this trip could not be higher for the future of the royal family’s standing in the region, warning: “I think it’s the biggest crossroads for the Commonwealth since its creation.”

Charles is expected to deliver three significant speeches during the trip, but will follow government advice not to issue a formal apology for Britain’s role in the transatlantic slave trade. The British government has also ruled out paying reparations.

The visit is expected to be met with protests over the monarchy’s colonial legacy and demands for a formal apology and reparations. It comes four years after the Prince and Princess of Wales’s controversial 2022 Caribbean tour, where images of the couple greeting Jamaican children through a wire fence sparked widespread criticism across the region.
Although Charles has gone further than his predecessors in acknowledging the monarchy’s historic links to slavery, he arrives in a region transformed.

Recent developments include a UN resolution, tabled by Ghana, declaring the transatlantic slave trade the gravest crime against humanity and calling for reparatory justice, as well as Jamaica’s unprecedented slavery reparations petition to the king, which is due to be heard by the UK-based privy council next March.

“I think his visit is pivotal,” Vernon said. “If the visit does not meet the needs and expectations of a lot of the Commonwealth heads, it raises a big question about the future of the Commonwealth. What’s the point of being in the Commonwealth when one of the biggest crimes against humanity, which has been recognised at international level, where you can’t even have a proper dialogue, conversation and exploration?”

The Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy, who chairs the all-party parliamentary group for Afrikan reparations, said the royal family and UK government had failed to reckon with a sea change happening across the world on this issue.

“I think it would be wrong to think that we can continue with platitudes. You’ve got ‘atrocity’, ‘deep regret’, ‘sorrow’, and now they’re going to say ‘darkest days’,” she said. “I think the king needs to realise that people wouldn’t keep raising it if what he was doing was anywhere near enough.
“You can tell that the Commonwealth means something to the monarchy, and I’m sure he would not want to be the monarch under which it crumbles.”

Prof Robert Beckford, a theologian at the University of Wolverhampton, said: “I think what’s at stake fundamentally is credibility: credibility in the monarchy and that leadership based on his ability to empathise and lead as the head of the Commonwealth. And the credibility rests on the ability to empathise with Caribbean history.”

While there were widespread calls for apologies, Beckford, also a broadcaster, said a “creative way” for the king to navigate the reparations debate would be to back a national truth and reconciliation commission examining Britain’s role in slavery.
“It would also provide us with the opportunity to take the nation on a journey into history, and understanding how slavery and colonialism operated as systems of extraction,” he said.

Protests over slavery reparations during royal visits to former colonies in the Caribbean are not a new occurrence. High Priest Richmond McKinney, a Rastafarian leader who is organising a protest during Charles’s visit to the Bahamas on Tuesday and Wednesday, was involved in demonstrations against Queen Elizabeth II in the 1980s.

“The cry remains the same: freedom, redemption and international repatriation. So we see it fitting to agitate and lobby and even have a protest against the crown now that it’s her son King Charles,” McKinney said. “You say you regret slavery, but your regret is not good enough. We want a full apology from you.”
Guyana’s president, Irfaan Ali, has made it clear ahead of the king’s visit that he wants progress towards reparations, beginning with an apology.
Currently, there are no formal agenda items on reparations at this year’s Commonwealth leaders’ summit in Antigua.

However, the chair of the Caribbean community reparations commission, Prof Sir Hilary Beckles, has said: “I can assure you that [for] everyone in the Caribbean right now, everyone who’s going to be at that meeting from the Caribbean, with an interest in the Caribbean, from Africa, and an interest in the global African movement, this will be the number one item on the table.”

Dr Niambi Hall Campbell-Dean, the committee’s chair, said: “We [are] spending hundreds of thousands of dollars to host the person who is responsible for the enslavement and colonisation of our ancestors, and what are we really getting out of it? So I think that the protests are twofold. It’s one for the king to be aware that we are still demanding that reparations be made, and then two to just [raise] awareness of more Bahamians and to cause us to really question our relationship to this crown.”
For Ribeiro-Addy, a successful trip would include an apology that quickly jumped to questions of “How do we move forward from this?”
“And the most important point to make is that the Netherlands’ king apologised. Their world didn’t end,” she said.

articles.title: The life and death of Jaysley Beck: how her mother turned detective – and took on the military
articles.summary: In 2021, the young soldier took her life after being sexually assaulted by a sergeant major, then sent thousands of messages by her line manager. She was just 19. Five years on, Leighann McCready is still searching for answers
body: When Leighann McCready phoned her 19-year-old daughter, Jaysley Beck, on 15 December 2021, she got no reply, but brushed away her worries. “Jays always, always answered her phone, but it was early, eight in the morning,” she says. Beck, an army soldier in the Royal Artillery, had been at a party the night before at her Wiltshire barracks. She was probably asleep.

It was a busy time, the Christmas countdown. Soon, Beck was expected to be back home in Cumbria, where her parents – McCready and Anthony Beck – own a village pub. McCready had already bought matching Christmas pyjamas for Beck and her older sister Emilli to wear on the day.

Beck had been preparing for the holidays, too. She had been Christmas shopping two days earlier, calling and consulting throughout the day with her mum, who was transferring the cash to cover it all. She’d bought presents for herself and her sister: a Gucci bag, a belt and a purse. For her dad, she’d bought tickets for a James Blunt concert for the two of them to attend together in February. At the end of the spree, Beck had messaged her mum: “We’re two so lucky girls aren’t we, Mum? Thank you, thank you, thank you. I love you with all my heart!”

Despite all this, as the hours passed that Tuesday in December, with still no word from Beck, McCready began to feel a deep foreboding. She knew that, in the preceding weeks, her daughter had been struggling through a strange and intense period of escalating harassment from her line manager. With this in mind, Emilli offered to call one of Beck’s friends at the barracks, who assured them that Beck was probably fast asleep. “He said he was five minutes away and he’d go and wake her,” says McCready. “That five minutes just seemed like forever. I continued ringing Jays’ phone – until somebody else answered it. The voice said: ‘Hello, can I ask who I’m speaking to?’ And I just knew. They didn’t even have to tell me.”

Gunner Beck had taken her life, alone in her bedroom. Her suicide threw a spotlight on the British army and the treatment, safety and protection of female recruits. For the last five years, ever since Beck’s death, McCready has fought for answers and accountability. She has found some, but believes there is still far more to uncover. At every step – the service inquiry, the inquest and a subsequent police investigation – McCready has been in the public eye, talking to the press, advocating for her daughter. Now, she features in a Stacey Dooley documentary, Death in the Barracks, which follows the family’s continued search for justice. She still can’t quite believe that any of it is real.

“Grief is not what you see on TV, where you instantly fall to the floor and break down in tears,” says McCready, who has worked for 30 years in the care sector, much of it as an end-of-life nurse. “The moment I found out, I automatically went from being a mum, a partner, a daughter, to quite literally feeling as if I was putting my uniform on. It was about protecting a family and guiding them. No matter how many interviews I do or how many times I see Jays’ photo in the news, it doesn’t register. That isn’t my daughter – and this isn’t my life. I call it my ‘invisible uniform’ and I have never taken it off.”

Beck had joined the army at 16. “As a child, I used to call her my baby muck-magnet,” says McCready. “She was a cheeky little chops – pulling out her pigtails, collecting snails. She loved helping her dad with DIY. You always knew when Jays was around.” Aged 15, she’d returned from a school careers day intent on joining the army. McCready wasn’t keen. “I hadn’t expected that in a million years,” she says. “I thought it was a phase, but she was determined. She put her heart and soul into it. I remember her running round the village wearing backpacks weighted with bricks to build her strength up. She was only tiny – probably a size six in clothes.”
After Beck’s initial military training, her family attended her passing in parade at Army Foundation College Harrogate. “It was magical,” says McCready. “I was a proud mum.”

Beck settled happily into army life – but in her final six months, that changed. In July 2021, at a training exercise, Beck was sexually assaulted by Michael Webber (then 39, married, and a battery sergeant major). She escaped, then spent the night hiding in her car. When Beck reported the incident to senior officers, she was advised not to be “a female troublemaker”, and was urged to think of Webber’s career, and his family. Eventually, after she reported it a second time, Webber was asked to write Beck a letter of apology. He was promoted shortly afterwards. This meant that, three months later, when her line manager, bombardier Ryan Mason, 32, began showing an obsessive interest in Beck, she had no faith in any complaints process, and nowhere to turn.

McCready had known all this as it happened. “Jays told me everything,” she says. Her daughter had even shared Mason’s messages on a family WhatsApp – he sent more than 4,600 in two months. The family had tried to advise and support her, but they were hundreds of miles away, and military protocol was a strange, sealed world. “When she was assaulted by Michael Webber, she’d said: ‘Get off me, sir.’” says McCready. “I remember my first reaction was: ‘How, Jays, did you call him “sir”?’ Some of it was over my head.”

In the days after Beck’s death, as their home filled with military personnel, McCready became determined to bring all she knew to light. “Jays was not going to be another statistic. She was not another ‘sudden passing’,” she says.

“I was not a ‘grieving mum’. You have to be stronger than that,” she continues. “I had to keep going for Jays and also for Emilli. What would she do if I broke? She’d crumble, she wouldn’t be far behind me.” Christmas was days away, so McCready asked Emilli how they should spend it. Should they even get a tree? “Emilli said: ‘Lets do the tree, and let’s still go to Auntie’s as planned for Christmas Day.’ So that’s what we did,” says McCready. “It didn’t feel right, but nothing would have felt right. I printed up a big picture of Jaysley and asked if I could put it in the tree so she’d be watching.” McCready didn’t touch any alcohol – in fact, she hasn’t had a drop since losing her daughter. “I don’t want alcohol to affect my emotions,” she says. She doesn’t watch TV either. “I don’t think it’s good for my mindset. I remember trying to settle down one night – I think it was [with] Gogglebox – and the first thing that was shown was a mortuary. I couldn’t turn it off quick enough.”

Her “invisible uniform”, her years in end-of-life care, guided all her decisions in those first weeks. “I knew I needed to be kind to my mind, to bubble-wrap it and protect it,” she says. “I chose not to see Jays after her passing and I don’t regret it. I know from my work that it’s just a shell left behind, and do I want to see my daughter’s shell? Instead, I can close my eyes and she’s that happy little girl – she’s smiling, she’s singing, she’s running round the block with her backpack on. I didn’t deal with the coroner – I didn’t want to know details.”

What she did want, instantly and urgently, was to visit Beck’s room in Larkhill garrison. She had to push for access. “I was told I was not allowed, so we had a meeting. I explained how much I needed this moment. I wanted to lie on my daughter’s bed. I wanted to know the last bit of music she played – Jays loved music, we always shared songs and playlists. What was the last bit of laundry she put in her laundry basket? How do her clothes smell?”

The family were finally allowed entry on 28 December, although they were initially informed that they had to be accompanied. “I said: ‘Absolutely not.’” McCready had another motive, too. “I needed to gather as much information to find out what happened,” she says. “I wanted the letter of apology from Michael Webber – I knew exactly where she’d filed it. I wanted her smart watch and her laptop. I got all of them. I did want her phone, too – but Wiltshire police had already taken that.” Months later, when the police had done nothing with the phone, McCready returned to Wiltshire to collect it, having argued successfully that she had paid for it – so it was in fact hers, not Beck’s.

“Not only had I put my invisible uniform on, in my mind, I was also becoming a detective,” McCready says. “I sat down with a roll of wallpaper and I did a timeline.” She also found a lawyer through the Centre for Military Justice. “We’ve been on this journey together and we’ve had to push for every single inquiry and investigation since.”

There have been some answers. After the inquest, the coroner’s summing-up report found Mason’s “intolerable harassment” and “the daily barrage of messages, calls and face-to-face encounters” to have been a significant factor in Beck’s suicide. As her line manager, Beck found Mason possessive and manipulative, setting the rota so that they were always together. He said that he loved her, composed messages that ran to essays, called her at night and engaged in lengthy conversations, sometimes until 4am (when she had to be up at 6am).

On 7 December 2021 – a week before Beck’s death – Mason and Beck had been staying in a hotel for a recruitment event when Beck left suddenly in the night, after calling a friend while in tears, who drove over and took her back to barracks. At the inquest, giving evidence, Mason said that he did not know the reason for Beck’s sudden departure that night. (He left the army the day after the recruitment event.)

The summing-up also found that the earlier mishandling of Beck’s sexual assault complaint against Webber had left her “with a feeling of injustice but, more importantly, [a loss of] faith in her ability to complain effectively”. After the inquest, Webber was charged with sexual assault and, last October, pleaded guilty. He was sentenced to six months.

Other factors were identified as “significant” by the coroner, foremost Beck’s “turmoil” around her intimate relationships. In November 2021, she had separated from her long-term boyfriend – although the two remained friends. She’d then embarked on an affair with a married sergeant. She was a 19-year-old girl, says McCready, making some mistakes and finding her way – and none of this explains why her daughter, who had never reported any mental health problems, should so suddenly end her life.

“Truth be told, there are still so many unanswered questions,” says McCready, “but I’m trying not to let them into my head. It won’t change anything for Jays. Instead, I’m trying to focus on changing things for the next people.” She welcomes MoD plans to tackle “unacceptable behaviours” in the military, including a Violence Against Women and Girls taskforce and a tri-service team, covering the army, navy and RAF, which will take serious complaints out of the single chain of command.

“It’s going in the right direction,” she says, “but it’s not enough. The reporting system has to be independent, separate from the army. I’m still contacted daily by soldiers, veterans and their families who have their own stories of rape, assault, bullying, harassment – and it’s not just females.” She hopes the Dooley documentary will encourage more to come forward, and she’s in the process of establishing a formal organisation, Jaysley’s Voice, to advocate on their behalf.

Meanwhile, Christmas – that most difficult anniversary – is coming. This year, McCready and Anthony are flying out to Thailand to meet Emilli and her partner, who now live in Australia. “We’ve promised each other that we’ll always be together at Christmas,” says McCready. “Emilli went travelling 10 months after we lost Jaysley, so we’ve met her in Vietnam, Singapore, Thailand, Bali. She keeps us busy, living the best life possible, which is exactly what Jays would have wanted for her. She’d have wanted that for all of us.”

Sometimes, McCready wonders if she has left any time and space for grief. She has rarely cried, she says, and opted against counselling. Could it all come crashing down? “I do ask: ‘Is this it?’” she says. “What am I waiting to feel like? Am I in denial?” Usually, though, she prefers to believe that Jaysley is close by, holding her together, protecting her from the worst of it, still on guard. “Maybe she’s saying: ‘This is how it will be for you, Mum, I’m not going to let you be hurt,’” says McCready. “For me, she’s still here.”

articles.title: Chinese markets lose trillions as race for AI supremacy with US takes its toll
articles.summary: Lack of profits and the threat posed by western countries are raising concern about the sustainability of Beijing’s AI boom
body: Trillions of dollars have been wiped from China’s stock markets in recent months amid increasing anxiety about the future of artificial intelligence, as Beijing races against the United States for dominance in the sector.

The STAR 50 Index, which tracks technology and innovation companies on the Shanghai stock exchange, has plunged 40% since June. Other indexes of major companies dropped by about 20% over the same time period.
The precipitous drop has wiped out $2.4tn from the Chinese stock market since May, according to Bloomberg.
AI stocks account for over 40% of the stock market value in China and Hong Kong, according to Goldman Sachs, meaning that any dent in value will send shockwaves across the whole domestic market.
Related: US bans use of China’s DeepSeek AI tools by government agencies

The fall suggests that despite the government’s best efforts to boost China’s technology industries, particularly those which harness the power of AI, the domestic economy does not have the power to sustain a booming market.

The Chinese government has invested heavily into AI, including a 60bn yuan state-backed AI investment fund which started pumping money into domestic developers this month. But Chinese consumers have proved stubbornly reluctant to part with their cash in many parts of the economy – including technology – meaning that many tech companies struggle to turn a profit.
The lack of profits is one of several reasons for the sell-off. Another is the threat of western countries, especially the US, extending bans on Chinese technology.

“This year, the profit margin is not as good as expected. And the US is raising rates. And China’s domestic demand is so weak,” said Dan Wang, the China director for the Eurasia Group. She said that there was a “general anxiety” among technology companies about whether or not the state-backed model would work in the face of weak consumer demand.

The US has banned humanoid robots from China, citing national security risks, and is thought to be considering a ban on Chinese components in data centres. China is heavily reliant on exports and restrictions in the US hurt its domestic companies, which struggle to sell enough products at home.

As China races with the US to pull ahead in AI, Beijing has doubled down on robotics – also known as embodied AI – as the key to rolling out the technology across society. Robotics is also seen as the answer to China’s demographic problems, such as the ageing population and the shrinking workforce.

But the demand for robotics is being driven by government agencies and research institutions, rather than everyday consumers, for whom the products are still too expensive and not yet practical for home use. Humanoid robotics and robotic dogs have been popular in the entertainment industry but are yet to be useful in home settings.
Shares in Unitree, China’s leading robot-maker, have halved since they started trading in August.

“It doesn’t look like embodied intelligence could turn into profits in the in the mass market,” said Wang. Thin profit margins, rising rates in the US, and weak domestic demand were all contributing to a “general anxiety” among technology companies, she said.

China’s government wants local investors to invest their money domestically. China has in recent months restricted overseas investment, with more regulations taking effect from 1 December, but these moves have not led to greater investment in the Chinese markets.

Wang added that there was still optimism in other technology sectors, such as AI research and satellites, the latter because their links to the military indicates long term state support for the sector. And globally the AI boom is expected to last for at least another year.

On Monday, US AI company Anthropic, which makes the chatbot Claude, filed paperwork ahead of a planned IPO that could be the biggest stock market debuts of all time. The company is expected to bring in as much as $100bn.

China has no such blockbuster IPOs on the horizon. And despite pressure on policymakers to introduce stimulus measures to boost investment, none are expected to be announced during a politically sensitive period in China.

This week the top officials in the Chinese Communist party are gathering for the fifth plenum, an important meeting that will lay the groundwork for next year’s 21st Party Congress. The Congress is expected to anoint Xi Jinping, China’s leader, for a fourth term. There is no appetite for risky or potentially destabilising policy measures before then, even if there is a chance they could boost the economy.
Any stimulus measure would be “high risk”, Wang said. “What if it doesn’t work out? Then whoever came up with that policy, that guy would be held accountable”.

articles.title: US bans vehicles from China’s BYD at Japan military base, calling them ‘unacceptable’ risk
articles.summary: US military says the restrictions on the electric vehicles at Kadena airbase also apply to delivery drivers and taxis
body: One of America’s biggest overseas military bases has banned vehicles made by the Chinese electric vehicle maker BYD over security concerns, the US military in Japan said on Tuesday.

The ban, which went into effect this week at Kadena airbase on the southern Japanese island of Okinawa, has fueled speculation that similar measures could be taken at other US military facilities as part of Washington’s crackdown on Chinese technology it suspects of being used to collect sensitive information.
“These vehicles present an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission,” Lieut Col Alli Stormer, a spokesperson for the US air force 18th Wing at Kadena, said in a statement.
Related: ‘BYD effect’: electric vehicle boom becomes unexpected tool to combat inflation

The restrictions apply to all BYD vehicles, including privately owned cars, taxis and delivery vehicles, reports said, adding that security personnel stationed at the base’s gates had been instructed to block BYD vehicles and instruct drivers to turn around.
Kadena, the biggest US air force base east Asia, would be directly involved in responding to a crisis involving China, Russia or North Korea.

Its inventory includes the powerful Typhon missile system, which is said to be capable of firing Tomahawk missiles as far as 1,600km, putting parts of China and Russia within striking distance. Kadena also hosts fighter planes and aircraft used for mid-air refuelling, surveillance and reconnaissance, according to its website.
The move comes amid concerns of potential information leaks via vehicle-mounted technologies such as cameras, sensors and GPS devices, South Korea’s Yonhap news agency said.

American military officials have not identified a specific threat, but the ban is part of wider measures taken by the US and other western countries to restrict Chinese smart technology in vehicles, mobile phones and other devices they fear could be used to “spy” on their owners.

In June the Pentagon added BYD to a list of 188 Chinese firms it believes have ties to the country’s military, drawing a protest from Beijing. The blacklist also includes the automaker Nio, e-commerce firm Alibaba and internet company Baidu.
The US defence department banned the sale and use of smartphones from Chinese companies Huawei and ZTE at military bases worldwide in 2018, again citing security concerns.

China has imposed similar restrictions on US-made Tesla vehicles. In 2021, it barred them from some government compounds due to security concerns over ⁠cameras installed on the vehicles. Beijing removed that restriction in 2024 after Tesla won an endorsement from the country’s top auto industry association.
BYD, which has not immediately responded publicly to the Kadena ban, overtook Tesla as the world’s biggest seller of battery-electric vehicles in 2025.

It is now expanding overseas, including in the world’s fourth-biggest auto market, Japan, where in July it launched its Racco electric minicar in the hope that the small, cost-efficient vehicle would carve out a place in a market dominated by domestic brands.

articles.title: Ukraine war briefing: Russia strikes Kyiv hours before truce begins in war-ravaged city Oleshky
articles.summary: Zelenskyy says ballistic missiles hit crowded areas with no military facilities nearby; truce comes amid reports of growing humanitarian crisis. What we know on day 1,707
body: Russian strikes on Kyiv killed one person and wounded eight, with mayor Vitali Klitschko saying medical facilities and an intensive care unit had been damaged in the late Monday attack. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said a ballistic missile attack had struck the grounds of a university campus in the Ukrainian capital. “The missiles hit very crowded areas, and there is not a single military facility nearby. This was a strike directly on the city, on its infrastructure,” he said on social media.

The strikes on Kyiv came hours before a truce in the ravaged Russian-occupied city of Oleshky was due to start, after months of reports that residents faced dire food, water and medicine shortages. The truce, aimed at allowing humanitarian aid into Oleshky, was to begin at 3am local time (0100 GMT). No end date for the truce has been provided. The city in Ukraine’s southern Kherson region has been caught in the crosshairs of fighting between the two sides since 2022, when it was seized by Russian forces. Neither Russia, Ukraine nor the US has said who would monitor the truce, or given details about the humanitarian operation set to accompany it. The Russian defence ministry said on Friday it would halt fire in the “Kherson sector” for the duration of the ceasefire. Ukraine has accused Russia of blocking residents from leaving, a charge Moscow has denied.

Before the latest strikes on Kyiv, Zelenskyy highlighted ​Ukraine was still waiting for US defence secretary Pete Hegseth to sign off on critical missile supplies. “We have been waiting for nearly a month for Mr Hegseth to sign off on missiles for Patriots and NASAMS. I instructed our team to raise this with the ⁠American side once again,” he said on X.

Romania said on Monday that a network “coordinated” from Russia was involved in starting a fire near an arms factory. The fire broke out on 14 September near an arms factory in the central city of Brasov and two Belarusians and a Ukrainian – residents in EU countries – were involved, authorities said. Two of them were “tracked down and remanded in custody in Germany while they were preparing to commit similar offences”, the office for organised crime said. The third is at large in Poland, it added. Russia’s embassy in Bucharest could not immediately be reached for comment but Moscow has repeatedly denied such accusations.

The attack in Brasov is the latest in a string of similar incidents in Europe, with Nato and the EU grappling with what they say is a “hybrid” campaign of sabotage and interference by the Kremlin aimed at undercutting Western support for Kyiv. On Tuesday, Russia’s defence ⁠ministry said ⁠its ​forces ⁠had struck a ⁠vessel ​in ‌the Black ‌Sea that was transporting cargo ‌for the Ukrainian military, according to Russian ​media ​reports. Before Tuesday’s attack, at ​least eight cargo ​ships have been hit off the coast of Nato members Romania and Bulgaria over the past three weeks. Some 34 sailors are reported dead or missing.

A Russian strike has damaged a major bridge spanning the Dnipro River in Kyiv, Klitschko said on Tuesday, following reports of multiple ballistic missiles launched towards the Ukrainian capital. “A strike hit the Southern Bridge. Metro infrastructure on the bridge was also damaged,” the city’s mayor wrote on Telegram. City officials said train services across the bridge had been suspended.

Ukraine’s military has begun using specialised aerial rescue drones to evacuate wounded soldiers from the battlefield, carrying two stranded troops to safety near the Russian border in the first such operations. The newly developed StarGate drone, a six-rotor aircraft fitted with an enclosed evacuation capsule, was used in two separate missions over the past week, the 475th Separate Assault Regiment, an elite unit, said on Monday. Developed by Ukrainian technology company SkyFall, the drone is intended to reduce rescue times from hours to minutes, reaching hard-to-access combat zones currently served by unmanned ground vehicles.

articles.title: Brazil: defeated Flávio Bolsonaro ordered to surrender passports
articles.summary: Far-right senator banned from leaving country as supreme court judge’s ruling makes reference to money-laundering case
body: The far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil and ordered to surrender his passports just hours after his dramatic loss in the presidential election to the leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva.
The ruling was issued by supreme court justice Alexandre de Moraes, the same justice who oversaw the trial of the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for attempting a coup.
Bolsonaro posted a video saying the decision was based on an interview his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, gave last Friday urging his brother to leave Brazil if he lost the election.

On Monday night, Bolsonaro’s party issued a statement acknowledging the election result, saying: “We recognise the presidential result proclaimed by the electoral court, but believe that the questions raised need to be properly clarified through a balanced and democratic political debate.”
Bolsonaro, like his father four years ago, has still not conceded defeat to Lula.
Related: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil

The court’s brief ruling regarding his passport only refers to a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating Flávio Bolsonaro over his possible involvement in a money-laundering scheme. The ruling orders him not to have any contact with his friend Willer Tomaz, a lawyer linked to betting companies that police suspect were being used to launder about £680m.
It also cancelled all of Bolsonaro’s passports, including the diplomatic one he holds as a congressman, and ordered him to hand them over within 24 hours.
Bolsonaro was the first to speak publicly about the matter, before Brazilian media were even aware of the judge’s decision.

In a video posted on social media, he said he had just left a visit to his father, who is under house arrest in Brasília, when “Lula’s federal police were at his door and in the middle of the street, and I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also prohibited from leaving the country”.
He added that, although his brother – who is in self-imposed exile in the US – told a US podcast on Friday that he favoured the senator leaving Brazil if he lost the election, “I never said that”.
When his Senate term ends early next year, Bolsonaro will be out of public office for the first time in 24 years, and therefore without the special jurisdiction afforded to officeholders.

He is under investigation in another criminal case, too, over what happened to the £20m he was captured on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father.
The Folha de S.Paulo newspaper reported that Flávio Bolsonaro had been persuaded to drop his plan to seek to annul the election, which he had announced after the result was declared on Sunday night.

Bolsonaro had claimed that the two-hour extension of voting – intended to allow voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport to cast their ballots – had harmed the election, despite the fact that his own campaign had also argued for an extension.
According to the newspaper, allies and lawyers told him his argument was legally weak.

Bolsonaro had still not publicly reversed his demand for an annulment, and in the same video he said he would file another case to have Lula’s ticket disqualified over alleged abuse of economic power, a similar case to others his legal team brought during the campaign.

articles.title: British politicians among international delegates barred from entering West Bank
articles.summary: Group was on visit to meet Palestinian children, farmers and civil leaders facing escalating violence from Israeli forces
body: An international delegation including British politicians has been barred from entering the West Bank on a trip to meet Palestinian children, farmers and society leaders facing escalating violence from Israeli forces during olive harvest season.

The delegation of 23 people, including four elected representatives, was drawn from countries including France, Spain, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Greece, Holland, Ireland and the US. It included the Labour MP Clive Lewis, the Scottish National party MP Lara Bird, the Scottish Greens MSP Kate Nevens and the former Labour MP Sam Tarry.

Lewis told the Guardian: “We were detained, taken aside and then interrogated. I use the word interrogated because people were shouted at. We were asked why we were going in, what was happening, why our stories were one way or the other. The bottom line was it was a deeply unpleasant experience.”

The delegates were set to participate in Progressive International’s Second Ramallah Congress, a gathering to oppose Israeli occupation in Palestine. The congress was organised by Progressive International in partnership with Birzeit University and includes a programme of meetings with Palestinian academics, students and civil society organisations.

Tarry told the Guardian that he thought the delegation had a “genuine chance of going across” into the West Bank but they were detained at the Allenby/King Hussein Bridge by Israeli forces in Jordan for nine hours. “They made a political decision very clearly based on the fact they didn’t want people to witness what’s been going on in the West Bank, especially ahead of the elections,” he added.

The exclusions occurred amid attacks by Israeli forces on Palestinian olive farmers and foreign press and activists in the region. International travel to parts of the West Bank is permitted but subject to military checkpoints. Earlier this month, Israeli media reported that the defence minister, Israel Katz, had instructed officials to pursue exclusion orders against activists travelling to Palestinian olive-harvesting areas.
Related: Guardian reporter filmed masked militants seconds before West Bank attack on French mayor

In the first two weeks of October, the UN aid coordination office recorded at least 160 Israeli settler attacks linked to the olive harvest, often under the protection or with the participation of Israeli forces.

Israeli forces attacked European diplomats and a French mayor accompanying Palestinian farmers, while about 80 olive-harvest volunteers, including US congressional candidate Brad Lander, were also recently detained.
Bird said in a statement: “I came to stand alongside Palestinians being attacked for harvesting olives on their own land. Instead, we were turned away at the border with no reason given.

“It is more important now than ever that we bear witness and show our solidarity. But we were prevented from doing so. If Israel has nothing to hide, why is it so determined to stop us seeing what is happening in the occupied West Bank?”

Laila Hazaineh, a political coordinator for Progressive International, said in a statement: “Despite escalating violence, our delegation remained determined to cross to Palestine to participate in the olive harvest, and actively engage with Palestinian communities and institutions. Every refusal of entry will only strengthen this determination.”
The embassy of Israel has been contacted for comment.

articles.title: Protest leaders urge French pupils to keep barricading their schools
articles.summary: Activists say struggle must go on until their ‘maximum’ demands are met over teacher shortages and building repairs
body: French children should continue to barricade their schools and take part in street protests, a student union said on Monday after the government announced a package of education measures to try to stem the crisis.

“Today we’re at the negotiating table, we’re able to negotiate with the government,” Pierre Sourzat of Les Lycéens told France Info television. “We’re in a power struggle and we still need to call for continued mobilisation to meet a maximum of our demands.”
Related: ‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policing
The government told high school student representatives it would cap some class sizes and review the university application system. But Sourzat said: “We want measures, not half measures.”

More than five weeks after the start of high school blockades in September, the government made the proposals to address the demands of what has become the biggest youth protest movement in years. It has been joined by trade unions and cost-of-living protesters in regular mass street demonstrations on Saturdays.

High school pupils had demanded an end to teacher and staff shortages and for repairs to decrepit school buildings that had collapsing ceilings, mould, broken toilets, a lack of chairs and windows that did not shut.
The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said some schools were so dilapidated they were “not fit” for teaching. He announced a government loan of €4bn to regional authorities to begin repairs.

Responding to complaints of overcrowded classes, Geffray said class sizes for 15-year-olds in the first year of high school would be capped at 28 in the 50% of schools in the lowest-income areas, increasing to all high schools next year. He said more teaching posts would be created and there would be a review of the French baccalaureate system.

The university application platform, Parcoursup, which has been described as opaque and unfair, will be changed in 2027 and replaced by a new system in 2028, according to the government. Parliament will hold a debate on the issue on Wednesday.
The higher education minister, Philippe Baptiste, said 15,000 extra student places would be created in higher education, focusing on vocational courses.

Louis Letoublon, who attended a meeting with the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on behalf of Les Lycéens, said: “Bravo to the high school students who have demonstrated. We’ve got something: the government is afraid and knows it must do something and listen to us. “Not all our demands were ⁠met. We’ll go on for as long as it takes.”
Baptiste said the government’s door was “open” for more discussions.
Several children have been maimed or seriously injured in the protests, allegedly by police explosive weapons. Hundreds of children have been arrested and held in police custody.

The authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrations after France saw its worst day of violence in years on 17 October, with looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings. Curfews have been put in place in certain cities, alongside protest bans. Protest routes were pushed to the outskirts of cities on Saturday when demonstrations passed off largely peacefully.

The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said there had been a new phenomenon in cities such as Nice and Montpellier at the weekend with ultra-right groups arriving in “organised formations” and targeting protesters. Eleven suspects are to face charges.
In a visit to Marseille on Monday, Emmanuel Macron said nationwide street protests were likely continue, and that the next day of street demonstrations on 31 October would also be a “day of risk”.

The French president said the looting and vandalism seen on 17 October should never happen again. Speaking to members of the police, he said it was “not normal” for the country to be in “such a state of turmoil” six months before a presidential election.
Macron steps down next spring and the far-right leader Marine Le Pen is leading the polls.

Macron said: “We will continue to hold the line. If we all do our jobs well, this movement will subside – because we will address legitimate expectations, and because order will be maintained. But nothing is a foregone conclusion.”
Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes on 17 October.

articles.title: Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election
articles.summary: Israeli prime minister increases alarmist rhetoric as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in polls
body: Benjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.
Related: What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s history
The Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.

“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in a social media post about Iran’s nuclear programme.

Israel’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration with Iran at a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.
Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.
Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.
On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convince Donald Trump to launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.
The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.
Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.

In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes had destroyed Iran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.

Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.

Most polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.

The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.

As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”

He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.

The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.

The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.
The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.

In the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”

The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.

In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.

In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.

“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”

Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.

His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.

Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.

articles.title: Middle East peace held back by US insistence that Iran is a threat, Oman’s foreign minister says
articles.summary: Badr Albusaidi calls for security pact involving Gulf states, Iraq and Iran with US no longer primary provider of security
body: The Middle East’s ability to solve its problems has been held back by America’s 50-year insistence that the Gulf states should view Iran as a security threat, Oman’s foreign minister said on Monday in a significant speech designed to break the deadlock over the region’s future.
Badr Albusaidi called for a non-aggression security pact involving all six Gulf states as well as Iran and Iraq. The US would in future no longer be the primary provider of security, he said.

He was speaking on the day high-level defence and intelligence officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia travelled to Tehran in an attempt to prevent a renewed outbreak of fighting between the US and Iran.

Tehran said the meeting also explored future security arrangements in the region. The high stakes were underlined by the sight of the Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, in Tehran weeks after Iran had struck Saudi infrastructure and as Iran-backed Houthis continue to send missiles towards Riyadh.
Albusaidi is the first Gulf leader to break ranks so explicitly by calling for the mainly Sunni Gulf states to form a security alliance with Iran, a long-term aspiration of Tehran’s.

Speaking at Girton College, Cambridge, he said the talks might be difficult and the proposal appeared counterintuitive, but “issues such as the strait of Hormuz have become impossible to resolve because external powers continue to define the terms of engagement, while regional powers are unable to take collective responsibility for making their own security arrangements and reach a consensus on them”.

He added: “What holds us back is that issues which ought to be handled at a regional level by the states of the Gulf themselves, are made more complex, more intractable and sometimes simply impossible to resolve because the region’s security arrangements are insufficiently developed.
“And they are insufficiently developed because they have relied for too long on the involvement of external powers.”

He said that for half a century Iran “had been systematically excluded from playing any meaningful role in the security arrangements of the region”. This had led to “profoundly negative consequences, not just for Iran, but for the region as a whole”, including the imposition of priorities on the region by external powers such as “the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf”.

He added: “Perhaps the most damaging of the priorities imposed on the region from the outside has been the requirement that Iran be excluded. Not just excluded. Worse. Positioned as the threat against which regional security had to be organised.”

Oman is on the southern side of the strait of Hormuz, with Iran on the northern shores. The two countries have reached a temporary agreement on how shipping traffic should be managed in the strait, but the plan is on hold until the US and Iran lift their respective blockades of the waterway.

Albusaidi also indirectly challenged Donald Trump’s case for a further attack on Iran by saying he believed the previous round of talks between the US and Iran in February, which Oman mediated, were “making significant progress, and that an agreement was within reach. We still stand by that judgment today.”

The Iranian foreign ministry has often proposed a security pact for the region in which Iran, as opposed to the US, plays a role. The US-Iran conflict may have reopened the debate among Gulf states about whether the heavy presence of US bases in their countries is a source of reassurance or insecurity. Oman is one Gulf state to have explored a regional security pact that includes Iran.

No Gulf state openly supported the US-Israeli attacks on Iran last year or this February, but some have covertly cooperated in the operations. Iran has sought to defend itself by attacking US bases and energy infrastructure in the Gulf states.
Related: Iran threatens to strike oil and AI facilities across Gulf if US and Israel renew attacks

The meeting in Tehran was taking place against a backdrop of continued Pentagon briefings about a major US military buildup in preparation for a possible assault after the midterm elections. Qatari mediators spent much of Sunday in Tehran seeking terms for Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz.
Israeli media reports claimed that the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has been trying to browbeat the military into provoking a war with Iran before the Israeli elections on Tuesday.
Donald Trump’s repeated call for Netanyahu to be re-elected only adds to the mood in the region that the US and Israel have the potential to be a long-term source of insecurity.

The idea of a security pact with Iran will be resisted in large parts of the Middle East after the damage Tehran has been prepared to inflict on the economies of the region, either directly or through the use of intermediaries such as the Houthis. Iranian hardliners increasingly say Iran’s security best lies in trying to assemble a nuclear bomb.
A pact that is likely to take many months to negotiate may also not be a solution to Washington’s demand that Iran reopen the strait of Hormuz before US sanctions are lifted.

articles.title: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil
articles.summary: A viral WhatsApp channel and student-led protests played a key role in the veteran Brazilian leftist’s election victory
body: After the first round of the Brazilian presidential election three weeks ago, the leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva reportedly told allies he could not understand how he finished second after a government he considered the best of his three terms.

A mood of dismay swept Brazil’s left, and because 9 million voters for the other candidates, all of them on the right, were expected to mostly transfer to senator Flávio Bolsonaro, analysts widely saw the far-right senator’s victory as certain.

Then, on the night after the election, students from the Fluminense Federal University took to the streets of Niterói, a city of 480,000 across Guanabara Bay from Rio de Janeiro, to protest against the return to power of a member of the Bolsonaro family, whose patriarch, former president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s father, is under house arrest for attempting a coup.

Two days later, another student protest took over downtown Rio and, in the days that followed, similar ones spread across the country in organic demonstrations that analysts and Lula himself agree gave new life to his campaign and played a decisive role in his historic comeback in the runoff.
Related: ‘Democracy always’: Lula vows no return to dictatorship in Brazil after election win
“I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” Lula said in his victory speech on Sunday night after defeating Bolsonaro.

Political scientist Fábio Vasconcellos said Lula’s victory, in which for the first time in Brazil’s democratic history a second-placed candidate overturned a first-round defeat in the runoff, could be explained by a combination of the streets, social media and the machinery of government – in recent weeks, Lula approved a “package of benefits” at the limits of what electoral law allows, including increasing and bringing forward payments from the main cash-transfer programme for poor families.
“The streets and social media almost overlap,” said Vasconcellos, a researcher with the Representation and Democratic Legitimacy group at the Federal University of Paraná.

Two days after the first round, congressman André Janones, a Lula ally, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army”, where Janones sent audio messages, videos – often beginning with shouts of “Guys, urgent!” – and dozens of daily instructions on how to make pro-Lula content perform well on social media.
The channel had 60,000 followers by the end of its first day and, by election Sunday, more than 10 million, and Lula’s digital reach overtook Bolsonaro’s.

In his victory speech, Lula called Janones “our general”, who had the role of “raising the morale of our troops every day”. The congressman’s relentless efforts, which included a 24-hour YouTube live stream on the eve of the vote, led to him being admitted to hospital last week – the only day the WhatsApp channel went silent.

Lula’s campaign also overhauled his online communications, and the incumbent, who turns 81 on Tuesday, began recording selfie videos despite not owning a mobile phone. On Sunday night, he said he had been given a phone and that “from now on I’m going to talk a lot to the Brazilian people, many times a day, directly”.
With the streets and social media, “the mood of defeat was gradually replaced by hopes of a comeback over those three weeks,” said Vasconcellos.
Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, said Lula’s comeback also represented “a broad rejection of the Bolsonarista project for Brazil”.
Related: Lula supporters celebrate shock election victory – in pictures

She has been interviewing undecided voters since May and said “the fear voters had, workers had, of losing rights and also of a possible concentration of power in Bolsonaro’s hands was very clear”, which meant that even people who did not like Lula voted for him this time.

Bolsonaro had won 56.1m votes in the first round and received 3.7 million more in the runoff. Lula, by contrast, went from 53.9m to 64.2m. The more than 10m-vote increase came both from persuading voters to turn out after historically high abstention in the first round and from convincing voters from other candidates, including Bolsonaro.

“Some undecided voters we interviewed said Bolsonaro was a playboy who sided with big business, while at the same time spontaneously saying that, if he won, there would be a dictatorship in which people would lose rights,” said Rocha.

Bolsonaro was also embroiled in several controversies recently, including saying he would use the new, even more conservative congress to change the constitution and “re-democratise” Brazil, as well as the two federal police inquiries in which he is under investigation over alleged corruption and money laundering.
Many analysts have also pointed to the weight of Lula himself. “If it were another candidate, Bolsonaro would already have won in the first round,” said political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles.

Marco Aurélio de Carvalho, Lula’s campaign manager, answered without hesitation when asked what explained the historic election fightback: “President Lula. We have a great statesman on our team. We have a star player. That’s what absolutely made the difference. I haven’t the slightest doubt about it.”
The question already occupying the minds of Brazil’s left is what happens next, given that Lula has said this was his last election.
“That is a very big challenge because, in the polling on this, Lula’s dominance is still very strong. There is no one in his party with the same leadership,” said Rocha.
Vasconcellos believes Lula’s re-election campaign, “from what we saw on the streets, offered the Brazilian left an opportunity for renewal”.
“Lula’s party can learn from what happened and find better ways to connect with young people and urban voters who feel their concerns are not being heard,” he added.

The Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips will be answering your questions about the election and the future of Brazil from 1500 GMT on Tuesday 27 October as part of our Conversations series. Email questions to conversations@theguardian.com

articles.title: France will lurch from crisis to crisis until it confronts its retirement timebomb
articles.summary: Letter: Amid widespread protests, Muriel E Cockcroft has sympathy for French youth but fears how much steam will be let out at the next convulsion
body: I’m writing in response to your editorial (The Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political moment, 19 October). While the focus is on Emmanuel Macron, let us not forget the hierarchical structure of French administration, from mayors to MPs to senators to prefects and heads of region. All are part of the government, but few stood up to bring leaky school roofs and missing teachers to national consciousness. I deplore the senseless destruction of shops and state buildings. But I also deplore the fact that students had to protest to be heard. In the many administrative tiers of this highly hierarchical country, no one acted and inertia prevailed.

Centrally, the government is financially challenged but refuses to acknowledge that having a huge deficit, an ageing population and a low retirement age are perhaps connected. Modest attempts to increase the retirement age also provoked violent protests. Financial tools for individual retirement remain complex and restricted. Thus, this sclerotic system presses on until the next crisis.

Neither side of the populist fringe offers a viable path forward. Marine Le Pen’s National Rally and Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise actively avoid confronting the retirement timebomb, preferring politically expedient promises over fiscal reality.

If a system treats retirement as a sacred cow even when the meaning of work is being redefined at lightning speed by AI, if it’s acceptable to have productivity grind to a halt in August because the wisdom of asking employees to all take four to five weeks off in the same month while we live in a 24/7 world is never questioned, and if that same system lets young people study by rote in leaky classrooms while offering its over-60s free social dinners, let us not be surprised if the pressure valve is showing signs of fatigue. My concern is how much steam will be let out at the next convulsion.Muriel E CockcroftFrance
